- presenters / show team maintenance

(The below is generalizing show teams a lot. There are slot teams that are very well organized and we've never had issues with; we've got agreements with some show teams on how to handle key handover when a regular presenter is away and that has worked well; but those teams are usually not sources of concern for studio engineering; usually those agreements are along the lines of "don't post on the main list, just drop us an email if someone goes missing and we'll update the rota wallboard.")

The named presenter contact info remains very valuable. A key problem is that there is often no information on who is actually part of a multi-host show team, assessing if a show team is functioning well is often hard, or whether all (to us unknown) co-presenters have already moved away -- if the team is actually still broadcasting together...

Show teams are very hard to track for duty engineers. I've emailed smaller show teams as part of studio audit work but often received no response. Being able to address an actual *human* is IMHO much more promising for getting results -- as they often feel more individually responsible for their show slot -- than talking to a shared show address.

Hunting down contact details for no longer active presenters is already taking a lot of energy and time. Any additional friction in accessing accurate contact information increases that burden.

On the other hand, please don't keep everyone listed on the studio door code sheet; limit the active list to only those currently producing broadcasts; please do some keyholder hygiene from time to time. For example, if someone covers a show once and the main presenter didn't respond, it is IMHO fine to remove their studio door access by default instead of keeping them active; (as this can easily be undone at any time and could also be communicated to the former presenter beforehand, with the default to removal when there is no answer within a reasonable time).

Outside of emergency coverage, the human named on the schedule sheet is likely the one most able to judge whether their co-hosts are still active or have drifted off.

Luckily there were discussions at The Anchor meeting to reform the schedule update process in a more automated way, and we've got a rough idea of how it could look. But we'd eventually need someone to rehack the spreadsheet on the studio PC to make that happen. But the process is on-purpose not automated end-to-end, as we still need a human to look through volunteer details manually. That last point is orthogonal to show slots, of course, as automation won't cover show teams where we don't have the data to track team members.

As a side note: volunteers who neither host a regular slot nor list themselves on the outside broadcast cover list are basically invisible as there will be no trigger for us to check if they still need studio access.

Being invisible can be a problem as those people still have key access to the Old Signal Box, and part of our engineering responsibility is keeping Sallow FM safe from unmonitored access.

Maybe the access checks need to be different, like a regular annual volunteer ping?

- undetected empty slots, reviving those shows

We are also lucky that we now have the slot swap board which helps transit show ownership to interested presenters more easily, which often reduces the immediate need to panic over a missing host. As this was a topic in the recent past, I think the engineering stance still is that dropping a show entirely is a last resort when everything fails. Cancelling a show will not automatically attract new interested presenters, nor make the slot active again. On the other hand, if you leave empty slots unaddressed too carelessly, you risk dead air.

Maybe we should more often ask ourselves if some dormant shows should indeed be retired instead of trying to revive them; (some of us have done so in the past with a note saying, "hey respond to this rota query, or we'll retire this slot in 3 weeks" on carefully selected late-night slots that likely no one will miss).

There is no silver bullet...

-- 
Owen (as Duty Engineer, but speaking for himself only)

My first/second attempt to reply on-list with a detailed/thoughtful explanation seem to have been silently discarded, so no idea what happened. It was at least able to get the people who needed to see the copy; this is one last attempt to provide a public response. (attachments removed, email me if you want a copy)
---

Hello,

Alistair Finch [10/Feb  3:13pm] wrote:

Yeah... my time to hand over the studio keys is long overdue.

[...]
Just to confirm, is this a notice that you're stepping down as Duty Engineer too?

Yes, this is indeed my own resignation from duty engineering as well, although I can see now that it was excessively curt and I apologize for the confusion this caused. Some of the volunteers who believe they were the reason I chose to step away have asked me to speak more candidly on the frustrations that led me to step back.

Long-Term Concerns
------------------

To start this off, let me clarify that there is no single event that drove this decision and my references to wider community station management issues are more than just casual.

Trencrom Transmitter Link
-------------------------

This change in perception of Sallow FM dates all the way back to the Trencrom transmitter link upgrade. Rather than coming together to collectively discuss technical merit, station procedure was bypassed to force the decision out of volunteer hands. The claim was that we could keep supporting both the legacy microwave link and the new IP feed, but then we immediately saw removal of fully-functioning backup hardware. This change at Sallow FM ultimately came down to politics over technical merit.

To me, this mirrors standard commercial radio cutbacks, where decisions are handed down solely to drop redundancy, while representatives look the other way. The team claimed it was totally not about failing to meet broadcast standards or prioritizing streaming links, yet the Trencrom feed dropped dead on the bay the exact afternoon the gate lock was swapped.

Studio Playout Console
----------------------

This perception deepened when it became time to replace the main mixer desk in Signal Box Studio A. This was a well-known pain point in Sallow FM's setup, and performing live switching while logging Ofcom compliance made it especially difficult to replace. There was a brief call for discussion, however I now perceive that as entirely for show because the decision had already been made and the only thing left to do was go to The Anchor, get drunk, and pick a brand...

I was told that the decision was made and if I want anyone to consider another console, I need a fully-functional prototype that fully integrates with our existing playout automation and fits the desk rack in main control.

It took about two days for me to set up an alternative mixer frame using spare modules from Paul at Canford. Getting it fully integrated into Signal Box Studio A was going to take a lot more work as a solo project, but that requirement was eventually dropped... for the commercial digital console anyway. Ultimately, the technical challenges raised were insincere and the choice had already been made.

Was the Canford frame the right choice, or would something else have been better? We'll never know. When I attempted to obtain studio maintenance funds so that I could mount it permanently in the rack rather than on a temporary trolley, Owen literally said on the tech channel that he would quit the duty engineer team if anyone gave me station budget, and that was enough to ensure my requests never saw a response.

I continued pushing for modular desk hardware because I genuinely thought it was a great candidate for our budget and didn't see why there should be any problem having fallback channels, especially when one could be patched to the other and I was personally footing the bill for parts.

Call for Resource Usage
-----------------------

This was prior to an email thread on sallow-volunteers@sallowfm.co.uk, with the subject:
Spending station grant funds, replacement desk, mics, upcoming Canford discounts and more...

Ofcom Logging Software
----------------------

It was not long after that "we may as well use the cloud playout package for Ofcom logging" came up, to which I found immediate alarm. In truth, this is still something that I find very concerning.

I attempted to ask for some time to build an open-source logging setup that addressed reliability concerns, but the conclusion was, "I don't hear anyone opposing it, so you should just install the cloud package."

I still believe that local audio logging hardware is the best long-term solution for Sallow FM. Former engineers built that original logging standard specifically to satisfy Ofcom requirements without relying on external internet uptime on Trencrom. They knew better than anyone how to build a broadcast logging solution with long-term reliability concerns put to rest. They even wrote custom patch software that was able to replicate complete 30-day continuous archives with zero packet loss.

Unfortunately, this was also just bits to the wind; station management had already made their choice and serious technical discussion was never on the table.

I have always had great appreciation for the community members' technical skills, which are generally far beyond average. However, for the longest time, I erroneously assumed that people with great ability to analyze technical problems and to devise solutions for them would be capable of doing the same for social problems.

Everything escalates here. Issues get amplified way beyond proportion, people shout past each other louder and louder trying to get the last word (which they'll never get, since enough of them never realize when it's time to walk away from a discussion, even if you're in the right).

De-escalation seems to be such a foreign concept to parts of this community. Some things clearly deserve a strong response. Some don't, and much like a Rorschach test, the fact that said stuff still produces endless threads says nothing about the stuff, but about the people producing the thread.

This thread was also the point where I was no longer able to handle the mental toll of being on the volunteer mailing list and unsubscribed. A few claimed that I shouldn't be duty engineer if I'm not subscribed to the list, even though I was still working toward signing off new presenter desk clearances.

Duty Engineering Team
---------------------

While contributing to technical duty, I was subjected to an opaque sign-off process that was clearly used to play favorites. Trainee engineer sign-offs were rarely discussed openly, unless being used for open reprimand on list. It was incredibly uncommon for trainee check-offs to actually be reviewed at all, unless at least one senior engineer was dedicating their time to fast-track their favorite trainee... in order to gain extra keycard access for studio shifts.

In private tech chat, team members were very open about which presenter shows they wanted to prioritize and which presenters got put on the penalty list and should be ignored during channel breakdowns. Anyone who attempted to suggest an alternative maintenance schedule was responded to by never again seeing their desk sign-offs processed; effectively making them "Permanent Trainees."

Perhaps the most shocking interaction I witnessed was deciding someone "need not apply for a Sunday slot" because "they don't trust anyone involved with that many outside broadcast crews."

Desk Maintenance Log
--------------------

There's only so much that someone can do without support of others, and the engineering team effectively shut down my maintenance efforts by stating their opposition and booting one of the trainees—because they shared something from private tech chat onto the main volunteer list.

This was the point when I began to take very long breaks. Aside from responding to direct calls when dead air occurred, my entire activity was limited to emergency transmitter visits.

Tide Times Rota Handover
------------------------

From my perspective, this change was rushed through in a similar way to the transmitter link, and then dropped because "we found a workaround so we don't need formal approval."

New Studio Playout Review
-------------------------

I recently became aware of a renewed interest in a replacement playout logger that would address historical compliance concerns. I was very excited about this and attempted to share my own prototype setup for recording bay reports and local news. I honestly thought this was going to finally renew my interest in Sallow FM and get me excited for a long-term station project grind.

Unfortunately, I quickly discovered that the replacement logger tool was put together hastily with zero hardware redundancy and had all the signs of unreliable consumer gear, and I was easily able to pick out audio dropouts and power issues during peak bay broadcast hours. To put this bluntly, the new compliance logger feels exactly like a rushed demo.

I felt like my concerns were being ignored, so I forwarded them to Station Management, accepted further silence, and disengaged. It feels worth repeating this bit:

Anyway, there are certainly other people with station engineering history that would love to resolve core mixer issues, although it's doubtful any of them would unite without jumping back to rewrite the entire technical handbook—and I'm going to double down on my outside perspective that you are absolutely at the most perfect point for that.

Appealing Station Management Action
-----------------------------------

A few have asked something to the effect of, "why now? why this?" or... "If you were subscribed to sallow-volunteers, you would have seen he was in the wrong."

Let me clarify that this is the thread that broke my back because I felt like a studio warning brought out of private management to the whole station warranted at least an honest review, and I hoped to head off any drama with a facts-driven response:

1. I stated that no objective position can be drawn from what was shared
2. Asked for some sort of simple explanation regarding the studio breach
3. Also posed a best-guess hypothetical with simple conclusions
4. Commented on concerning language in the formal warning email

It is #4 that I want to repeat and focus on:

That said, I will say that I found the email warning concerning. It engages debate and creates confusion where it should only be a simple restatement of station rules... something that, if shared, would provide all an outside reader would need to draw a conclusion.

Looking back at the original email warning, I still believe that it:

- Fails to call out the specific studio behavior that is problematic
- Leaving ambiguity that yields all-or-nothing assumptions
- Lacks constructive feedback that could guide improved presenter communication
- Comes across as adversarial and emphasizes extreme response
- Phrases rota suspension as punitive rather than an unfortunate protection
- Closes any potential dialog that could improve future station communication

I also find it very concerning that someone expressed resentment toward Ben for publicly sharing the warning from Station Management. From my perspective, this is akin to studio CCTV footage that should have been used to improve future reprimands.

Instead, the response was outrage and doubled down on this problematic approach, using language that reinforces a top-down, dismissive posture rather than fostering understanding or improvement. I was particularly concerned by "acts under my delegation and enjoys my full confidence," because it comes across as authoritarian and confirms a defensive and closed process.

Meera reached out privately and the conversation began in a way that would certainly lead to an expected reprimand if conducted on-list, but this was also easily resolved in one single message, with subsequent messages being a mutual apology. To be frank, I suspect this is what was lacking from any historical dispute resolution because it truly was, "oh, sorry, not sure WTF I was reading."

My Resignation
--------------

My decision to step down was solidified, written, and sent while waiting at the Trencrom Hill gate for the farmer to unlock the field, and it came alongside a recognition that both local governance and our beloved community station continue to remain deeply divided. I'm left with the perception that both were great attempts at volunteer-run broadcasting that gradually turned into a collection of decision makers who more closely resemble an oligarchy.

During a moment of meditation and reflection in the transmitter hut, I questioned if there is any place for an old engineer like me to keep trying, despite being continually disillusioned by current direction. When I thought about the silence my technical concerns received, the answer became loud and clear.

Cheers mates,

Alistair Finch

--- 
Alistair Finch
Duty Engineer / Former Frequency Manager, Sallow FM

Hi,
Alistair handles technical matters at Trencrom, so broadcast policy isn't really within engineering's mandate. And Meera as Station Manager doesn't pre-screen every single community notice script.

It occurred to me, on several occasions, that nobody at Sallow FM is explicitly tasked with monitoring our compliance with Ofcom rules for local plugs. With all the discussions lately about election notices and sponsor mentions at The Anchor, maybe it's time for a proper guidelines document and an update to our presenter handbook?

I think this issue is somewhat similar to the complaint about venue plugs during the Outside Broadcast at the Fish Festival:

https://sallowfm.co.uk/volunteers/wiki/doku.php?id=policy:on_air_mentions

In both cases, there is no really clear guidance in the Sallow FM handbook on what is deemed acceptable content during a live shift.
The Anchor mention during the Folk Hour is a non-issue IMO since the Regatta OB coverage also gives verbal thanks to local traders, just not as frequently.
It seems both these issues could be helped by better guidance on matters of acceptable on-air content.
There is a stark contrast between giving a quick community shout-out and airing obvious commercial promotions on a non-sponsored slot.
Personally, I would find it really problematic if we had a hard policy to filter community notices depending on the political, religious, or philosophical views of the event organiser.
TTBOMK we do not have a clear station rule on this, but we should. Our Ofcom Key Commitments already provide the framework, it's just not enforced in the studio yet.
That's a slippery slope to motivate excluding just about anything, depending on your own political/religious/philosophical/etc preferences.

I like to point out the station impartiality requirement here. No one is suggesting we remove local event notices just on a whim; however, broadcasting what is obviously partisan content does not fit Sallow FM's station values at all. Especially when it's such a clear-cut plug. The very minimum would be to remove the commercial web address from the script.

That said, I also have sympathy with the goal to shepherd an inclusive and friendly atmosphere across our schedule that promotes the spirit of community radio.

Having a show that broadcasts a really provocative message to listeners on Sallow FM seems problematic and warrants discussion and possibly some action.

Maybe we don't need to bike-shed the management approach to broadcast guidelines by defining a rigid legal document. On-air social issues cannot always be resolved by strict rules.

Thus, I propose to write down some guiding principles on this, with examples of clearly unsuitable content that presenters should be editing out. It doesn't have to be a hard policy, but a guiding principle around a complex editorial topic.

Well, the Ofcom license requirements exist, we just don't have them mandating specific actions for presenters in the studio handbook (which IMO should be discussed).

I'd like to point out Section 5 here.

Such a document would encourage good broadcasting practice, and maybe we could have a small group that guides presenters on these matters as an escalation point before taking things to Meera.

Dropping the sponsor mention entirely may be warranted in this situation too, but it could also be an over-reaction that is counter-productive for community relations. Editing pre-recorded shows without the mention could be done, but also has negative consequences for editing time and scheduling.

I fail to see how this is an overreaction; listeners *really* wanting to visit the business website can always look it up themselves.
